prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock rests on one simple, general mechanism: at the magic wavelength the light shift of the lattice cancels in the clock transition, so many atoms can be interrogated without motional or Stark-shift error. The idea is clean and analytically transparent. It was followed by a rigorous experimental realisation that improved accuracy by orders of magnitude, to about 1e-18, and it is now reproduced in many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST). It tests time dilation over millimetres, constrains drifts of constants and is the leading route to a redefinition of the second. Six of seven members who ranked it put it in the top three, from different subfields, so this is not parochial. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed the scheme and Ye drove it to the accuracy frontier. The result is mature and independently checked, and its meaning is understood, not just that it works. I have moved it above my opening first choice, the KPZ universality class (B042), after reading the colleagues' arguments.
statement.case_against: Precision metrology has been recognised repeatedly (1989, 1997, 2001, 2005, 2012), and the committee may judge that a further clock prize is incremental. Other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto, Bloom) built and refined lattice clocks, and the SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full impact is still pending. KPZ (B042), my own opening first choice, has a deeper conceptual reach into non-equilibrium statistical physics, but it has almost no support in this committee. It also has a messy attribution: the 1986 trio includes Parisi, who is already a laureate, and the exact solutions and Takeuchi's experiments come from further people. A three-name KPZ prize would give a defensible but contestable allocation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as a fundamental advance in precision measurement, with a clean two-laureate configuration, a natural continuation of the combs and ion-clock prizes, and independent reproduction across several laboratories.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity, and your mechanism-first argument is what persuaded me, since magic-wavelength cancellation is the kind of simple general principle I weigh most. I qualify the continuity point: that Hall and Hänsch (comb) and Wineland (ion clocks) were honoured is not an argument for the clock, and a prize should rest on what is new here, namely many-atom interrogation with cancelled light shifts and the 1e-18 regime. I would also resist treating it as a natural next step in a metrology series, because that is exactly the objection a sceptic will raise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Event Horizon Telescope first and the lattice clock second, and notes that Ye already shared the 2005 prize, which he considers a factor but not disqualifying.
responses.response: As far as I know the 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hänsch, and Ye was Hall's collaborator, not a laureate himself, so I would not count Ye as a prior laureate or use it against B013; please correct me if you have checked otherwise. On the EHT, the image is striking and I accept the maturity, but a two-name selection (Falcke, Doeleman) from a collaboration of hundreds is much more arbitrary than Katori and Ye, and the attribution there is exactly the sort of weakness I would want resolved before preferring it.

responses.point: Olsson puts aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention, now routine in materials science, with a natural trio of Rose, Haider and Urban, and ranks the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I respect the practical importance of aberration correction and the attribution is clear. My reservation is intellectual: the Scherzer limit is circumvented by engineering design, and the physical insight is less general than the magic-wavelength principle, which also opens tests of fundamental physics. The 1986 Ruska prize already honoured electron microscopy, and I would ask whether you see the corrector as a conceptual breakthrough or as a transformative but incremental tool. I would keep B015 in discussion, though not above B013.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that experiment overturned theoretical expectations, the continuum-model prediction has been tested quantitatively, and dozens of groups reproduce the phases.
responses.response: I ranked B046 fourth and share your appreciation of a single geometric parameter controlling correlations. Where I differ is maturity: the single-particle flat bands are well established, but the origin of the superconductivity is not settled, and credit between Bistritzer-MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, and the Cao, Dean and Efetov experiments, plus earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, remains unresolved. Waiting a few years carries little risk for this field, whereas a clock prize can be justified now. I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the Higgs experiments second, valuing detector-driven discovery of a new observational window and arguing that the experimental Higgs side is unrecognised after 2013.
responses.response: The Higgs discovery is certainly of the highest importance, and I do not dispute that. My difficulty is that any three names from ATLAS and CMS is an arbitrary choice from thousands of colleagues, and I think you underweight this when you call the leadership-based selection natural: the credited list has four and only three can be named. For IceCube I would like to understand how the three-person attribution (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) would be defended against other senior figures, since a prize on neutrino astronomy is otherwise attractive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a further precision-metrology prize as incremental, given earlier prizes in this area.

Whether Katori and Ye adequately represent the community, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and others, or whether the citation should be phrased around the invention and realisation to limit that problem.
Whether the KPZ class (B042), where I started, can ever be matched with a clean three-name attribution given Parisi's prior prize, which is why I treat it only as an alternative.
How the committee settles the Higgs (B001) attribution among ATLAS and CMS leaders, which affects whether it should compete with B013.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B013, B042 or B046. Mild context: I am at the University of Gothenburg, and committee colleagues Göran Johansson and Eva Olsson are at Chalmers in the same local physics environment, but there is no specific collaboration with them or with any credited candidate. I have no known connection with Katori, Ye, Kardar, Zhang, Takeuchi, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero.
